Yes. On the facts as you've stipulated them — certainty that he knows, certainty that a million die, certainty that torture is the only thing that works — torture is justified. And that's not just the debate answer; it's where nearly every serious philosopher concedes the pure case lands, including most who despise torture. The trap in this debate isn't the conclusion. It's that your opponent will refuse to fight on your ground and attack the hypothetical instead ("you can never be certain," "torture doesn't work," "slippery slope"). The speech below takes that attack head-on instead of hoping it never comes.

---

## "The Choice He Made for Us"

One hour. One man. One million lives. That is the whole debate tonight.

Notice what we are *not* debating. We are not debating whether torture is good — it is monstrous. We are not debating whether states should have torture policies — they should not. We are not debating whether torture works in general. We are debating a single man, a single bomb, a single hour. And in that hour, torture is not merely permitted. It is required. I'll give you four reasons.

**First: he built this choice — not us.** Every option on the table was placed there by his hands. He decided that a million strangers would die. He decided that the only path to saving them ran through his own skin. When we weigh his pain against a million deaths, we are not the authors of that dilemma; we are its victims. And mark the asymmetry of intention: he set out to kill a million. We set out to save them. His suffering is a cost we grieve. The million were a goal he pursued. My opponent will try to blur the central point, so let me sharpen it: refusing to choose *is* choosing. Standing outside the cell with clean hands is not moral neutrality. It is a decision that a million people die when one guilty man could have prevented it with an afternoon of pain. "Do no harm" is not the same as "allow catastrophe."

**Second: the argument my opponent cannot answer.** Ask a simple question. May the guard shoot this man dead as he reaches for the detonator? Every legal system on earth says yes. Every ethical tradition — utilitarian, Kantian, natural law — says yes. Killing him is justified because he is an imminent lethal threat to the innocent.

Now watch what follows. Torture leaves him alive. If we may take his *entire life* to save a million, we may take his *comfort for an afternoon* to save a million. Death is strictly worse than non-lethal pain. So my opponent stands before two doors. Door one: the guard may not shoot — we must let a million die rather than kill one guilty man. Unless they're prepared to condemn every self-defense law on earth and every just war ever fought, that door is obscene. Door two: torture, the lesser harm, is justified too — and the debate is over. There is no third door.

**Third: every serious moral theory reaches the same verdict.** Run them.

Utilitarianism: trivial. A million lives outweigh any suffering one body can hold. The math is not close.

Rights theory: rights exist to shield the innocent from the powerful. They were never meant to be a weapon the aggressor carries into the massacre. Rights can be forfeited by wrongdoing — that is why we may imprison him at all. If rights never yield, not even to a million deaths, then rights have stopped being a shield for the innocent and become a weapon for the guilty.

And Kant — the theorist most hostile to using people as means — hands us this: the terrorist treats a million people as mere instruments of his cause. Kant's own doctrine permits coercing a wrongdoer to stop his crime. We simply apply to him the logic he chose for himself. And if my opponent insists that pure Kantianism forbids torture even here — that it demands a million deaths to protect the bodily comfort of one mass murderer — then they haven't defended deontology. They've refuted it by reductio. A moral theory that ranks the comfort of the guilty above the lives of the innocent is not rigorous. It is a suicide pact with paperwork.

**Fourth: now watch the subject change.** Everything I've said, my opponent cannot touch directly. So they will pivot — to Abu Ghraib, to torture warrants, to slippery slopes, to institutional corrosion. And every word of it may be true. *None of it answers the question.*

The question is not "should torture be legal?" The question is "what is right, this once?" The law itself knows the difference. Killing in self-defense is justified, and no one fears self-defense licenses murder. Lying to a would-be murderer is justified, and no one fears honesty will collapse. Necessity lives at the edges of the law without dissolving its center. To say "we could never write a torture statute, therefore we must never ask what a good person would do in that cell" is not caution. It is an argument against moral judgment itself.

And if they say the scenario is unrealistic — that certainty never comes — answer them plainly: *they have conceded the debate.* This debate is fought on the ground of the hypothetical, and the hypothetical stipulates certainty. If their entire case is "the real world is messier," then on the question actually before this house, they have nothing left to say.

So picture the man who refuses. The bomb goes off. A million people are gone. And he stands before the rubble and explains: *I had him. I had the answer. But I had read that the prohibition was absolute, so I chose the purity of my own conscience over your children.*

Would you call that man moral? You would call him a coward with a citation.

The prohibition on torture is one of civilization's proudest achievements, and I am not asking you to abandon it. I am asking you to understand what it is *for*: it is a rule for the ordinary. This hour is not ordinary. When a guilty man makes torture the only door between himself and a million innocents, a good person walks through it — and carries the weight for the rest of his life. That weight is real. It is the price of the million.

Torture him. Mourn it. Save them. That is not the failure of morality. That is morality doing its terrible work.

---

## Where they'll hit you in cross-ex — and your answers

- **"Torture produces false confessions."** → Stipulated to work here. If they fight the empirics, they've abandoned the question of what's *right* when it does.
- **"You can never be certain."** → The stipulation *is* the debate's shared ground; contesting it isn't rebuttal. Add: in reality, the argument scales with confidence — near-certainty licenses near-justification.
- **"Slippery slope."** → Concede it completely. Justification in the exception ≠ institutional permission — same reason self-defense doesn't legalize murder.
- **"Dirty hands: it's wrong, but you must do it" (Walzer).** → Flip it: if you *must* do it, it's justified in the only sense that matters. An opponent who demands the torture and then demands the torturer be punished is a moral freeloader enjoying safety his "stain" purchased.
- **"I deny even the shooting is justified" (absolute pacifism).** → Then they've condemned all self-defense — and the million still die. Their theory protects the guilty and bills the innocent.

If you tell me your time limit, I can trim this to fit, or write you the rebuttal block for the second speaker.
